newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Hope among the ruins of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hope among the ruins of Kabul.

text.p: After four years as the front line between Afghanistan's warring factions, Kabul is a city of ruins.
The war has moved north -- albeit only 20 km (12 miles) -- and people are trying to rebuild their lives and their city.
They face a huge task.

"To find a parallel to the destruction in Kabul you would have to go back to Dresden," says Greg Wilson of the United Nations agency Habitat. Dresden was almost razed to the ground under some of the heaviest bombardments of World War Two.
"Kabul is three to four times as badly destroyed as Beirut, and four to five times as badly destroyed as Sarajevo," says Wilson.
"In terms of residential areas probably 50 percent of the housing has been destroyed. That rises to 90 percent in some districts."

The battle front cut a swathe running from east to west through the middle of the city. Hundreds of thousands of rockets, rocket-propelled grenades, mortar bombs and artillery shells pounded what were once Kabul's most heavily populated areas into rubble.
With the help of the United Nations and the non-governmental organisations, the Afghans are starting to rebuild Kabul, but the level of destruction means that they are largely starting from scratch.
In Kabul's old city, which bore the brunt of much of the fighting, people are rebuilding some of their basic infrastructure.

They have rebulilt stairways and flood drains. "We have had two big floods this year, and they washed some houses away, so we rebuilt the flood drains." said Mohammed Taki Haideri, head of the local rehabilitation council.
"We provided the labour and the stones and Habitat provided the cement, gasoline for the trucks and technical assistance," said Haideri.
According to Wilson, such examples of community participation are the most cost-effective way of rebuilding the city. But, he says, there is still much work to be done.

"All the basic services have been destroyed including roads, housing, the electricity system, drainage, public transport...It is almost impossible to earn a livelihood here because the basic infrastructure is no longer in place." says Wilson.

Mains electricity has recently been reconnected after two years. It was a major task: cables had been shot off the pylons and sold for scrap and the local distribution system still needs extensive repairs before all houses are connected to the grid.
The restoration of electricity should blunt some of the hardships caused by trying to heat houses over the bitterly cold winter.
As reconstruction gets under way one of the biggest problems will be the huge quantity of mines and unexploded munitions.
"There is an extraordinary amount of unexploded ordinance around." says Wilson, "Maybe 20 percent of all the incoming munitions didn't explode, and they are still lying around in the piles of rubble.

"There have been large numbers of casualties, many of them children, but adults also. When adults go back and start the process of rebuilding they have to go through the rubble trying to rescue bricks and beams," says Wilson.
Wilson says that despite the problems, Afghans will rebuild their city.
"Given some resources, people here have shown that they can get back on to their own feet with technical assistance from agencies like the United Nations and non-governmental organisations." he said.
According to Wilson, the lack of resources is a major stumbling block on the road to reconstruction.
"Afghans are a very hard-working people. We've shown it can be done, but we need more resources.

"We don't know the full extent of the damage or the cost of rebuilding the city, but we are talking billions of dollars. The sort of money we have available now is nothing like that; we are only making a tiny dent."
